title: Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an affordable structural system that confines collapse after the loss of any one primary load-bearing member to a declared local region. Within a specified class of buildings, loading conditions and construction tolerances, removing a column or a defined segment of bearing wall would not trigger collapse beyond that region. Local damage would remain possible; the intended advance is to prevent it from spreading through the structure.

The research objective is a simple structural mechanism or general design principle that gives the building this containment property without a separate project-specific study of every possible member-removal scenario. Existing performance-based approaches already pursue containment by assessing structural response to defined damage. The proposed advance would be a broadly justified system property covering every qualifying single-member loss within its declared scope. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Disproportionate collapse occurs when local structural damage leads to a collapsed area much larger than the initiating damage would suggest. The supplied historical accounts connect robustness research and guidance to Ronan Point, the Murrah Building and NIST’s World Trade Center investigation. These examples motivate limiting failure propagation, although their initiating events and damage patterns differ and should not be treated as equivalent single-member losses.

Conditional assessment: if ordinary buildings could acquire reliable single-member collapse containment at ordinary construction cost, robustness could become an inherent property of the structural system. The direct consequence would be containment following a qualifying member loss. A sufficiently general, validated design principle could also substantially reduce reliance on individual removal-scenario studies, making this form of robustness easier to apply consistently. Those consequences depend on demonstrating coverage of the stated building class, loads, member locations and construction tolerances.

Protection against every blast or impact would not follow from single-member containment. One event can destroy several members, damage connections and impose additional loads; NIST’s account describes the Oklahoma City bombing as initially destroying three columns. Protection against an event would therefore be conditional on its damage and loading remaining within the system’s demonstrated envelope.

Scope synthesis: fire, foundation failure and simultaneous loss of multiple members remain separate challenges unless explicitly included in an expanded demonstration. Confining structural collapse would also not establish that the building remained undamaged, habitable or immediately usable. These limits preserve the distinction between preventing failure propagation and providing comprehensive protection from an extreme event.

missing_breakthrough.text: The sought breakthrough is a validated mechanism or structural argument connecting local member loss to a firm bound on subsequent collapse throughout a declared building class. The supplied accounts of ASCE/SEI 76-23 establish a mitigation framework involving performance objectives and assessment of defined damage. They do not establish the proposed ordinary-cost, any-member containment property, nor do they establish that no existing system possesses it.

Engineering synthesis: an alternate load path must remain usable after the original support disappears. Ties and catenary action—the ability of connected members to carry redistributed load through tension—are relevant mechanisms, but their presence alone does not establish containment. The design must account for the forces and deformations produced by sudden support loss, the strength and deformation capacity of connections, and the possibility that redistribution overloads adjacent members or connections. A general principle must explain why propagation stops, rather than simply identify another route for the load.

Proposed coverage challenges include corner-column removal, removal of defined bearing-wall segments, and member loss in a structure already affected by an earthquake. These cases challenge a design to work across different support geometries, structural systems and damage histories. They are useful targets for investigation, but the supplied evidence does not establish that all such configurations are comparatively unreliable or that existing approaches uniformly fail in them.

The earthquake interaction requires particular care. The available abstract of the December 2025 review identifies a gap in systematic treatment of earthquake-induced progressive collapse within standard seismic design procedures and examines whether special seismic detailing provides sufficient redundancy and integrity. The available material does not supply the detailed conclusions needed to assert that such detailing is generally inadequate.

Practical research requirements also remain to be defined: what counts as one wall segment, how far local collapse may extend, which construction errors are tolerated, and what additional cost qualifies as ordinary. A mechanism that works only with exceptional precision, extensive strengthening or unusually expensive connections would not meet the proposed affordability and ordinary-construction objective.

current_state.text: On June 5, 2023, NIST announced ASCE/SEI 76-23 as the first national building standard of its kind. Its stated purpose was to keep isolated structural failures from propagating into collapse of an entire building or a major part of it. NIST described a performance-based approach that sets structural goals while allowing designers to choose how to meet them. Its account also describes physical removal scenarios and experiments used to validate simulations, demonstrating an established research and assessment approach rather than a universal containment guarantee.

NIST described use of the standard as voluntary in June 2023. Engineering News-Record’s June 11, 2023 report stated that building-code use was not required and attributed to committee chair Donald Dusenberry the expectation that it would not become required. These are dated accounts, not verification of adoption in every jurisdiction or of adoption status on November 1, 2026. The standard itself was not retained in the supplied source collection, so this record does not claim an independent examination of its detailed provisions.

Mohammad Ashrafy and Reza Aghayari’s review, published December 18, 2025 in Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering, addresses progressive collapse of reinforced-concrete buildings during earthquakes. Its available abstract states that earthquake-induced progressive collapse has not been systematically included in standard seismic design procedures and says that the adequacy of special seismic detailing is critically evaluated. The retained material is a subscription preview. It supports that narrower account of the review’s scope and integration gap, but does not establish its detailed findings about the effectiveness of special detailing.

Evidence boundary: no prestressed-steel test evidence is supplied to substantiate the earlier assertion that corner-column removal remains a demonstrated weak case in those tests. The supplied material also contains no demonstrated ordinary-cost guarantee covering any single primary-member loss. Because the freshness record is empty, this establishes a limit of the available evidence, not proof that the capability remained unavailable throughout research and practice as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test ordinary multi-story structures representing a declared building class, including a frame with a corner column and a bearing-wall building. Suddenly remove several different primary members under specified gravity loads and a stated lateral load. Define the permitted local collapse region before testing, including an explicit boundary for wall systems; one bay could be a proposed frame boundary where appropriate. Any collapse must remain within that region. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Sudden primary-member removals confine collapse within predefined local regions

completion_criteria.text: Use independent specimens for different removal cases, or a protocol that explicitly measures and accounts for accumulated damage. Repeat the challenge with specified construction errors representative of ordinary practice. State the member locations, load levels, removal times, connection details, tolerances and measurement methods so that independent teams can reproduce the tests and assess whether containment depended on exceptional specimen quality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible removal tests account for accumulated damage and construction errors

completion_criteria.text: A general any-member claim would additionally require a validated structural argument covering the declared building geometries, primary-member locations, connections, load combinations and construction tolerances. Experiments and validated simulations should challenge the assumptions and boundary cases of that argument. Finite tests establish demonstrated breadth; they do not establish literal universality. Tie-force calculations alone, or one successful column-removal test on a regular frame, would not satisfy this proposed evidentiary threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Validated structural argument covers any-member loss within the declared scope

completion_criteria.text: Practical acceptance would require a stated cost baseline and evidence that the system can be built using ordinary construction methods within the claimed cost range. The demonstration should identify the limits beyond which containment is unproven, including any exclusions for prior earthquake damage, fire, foundation failure or multiple-member loss. A successful result would support a bounded claim of collapse containment, without automatically establishing continued occupancy or repairability.
completion_criteria.label: Ordinary construction meets claimed costs with containment limits stated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: STR-07, “Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism,” has potentially substantial overlap with STR-12 because both concern preventing an unwanted structural failure mechanism. STR-12 specifies a trigger and outcome: loss of one primary member must not cause collapse beyond a declared local region. The supplied roster does not define STR-07’s mechanism or scope, so the earlier characterization of it as merely controlling a crack path in a brittle assembly cannot be retained as established. The entries remain distinct pending a fuller comparison.

Roster-based comparison: STR-10 concerns ordinary buildings remaining undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes. STR-12 permits declared local damage and collapse while requiring containment after a qualifying member loss. STR-04’s seismic cloaking and STR-11’s passive damping address earthquake exposure or resonant response and could reduce demands that initiate damage. Their stated objectives do not, by themselves, demonstrate containment once a primary member has disappeared.

Roster-based comparison: STR-01’s flaw-tolerant, high-specific-strength members address material and member performance, while STR-03’s complete cast-mineral primary structure addresses what can constitute the load-bearing system. Either could supply components or a structural platform for STR-12, but member strength or material completeness alone does not establish building-wide load redistribution and collapse containment.

Roster-based comparison: STR-02’s autonomous restoration, STR-05’s reprogrammable mechanical state and STR-06’s growth and remodeling could intersect with adaptation or recovery after damage. STR-12 requires containment during the response to member loss, so later restoration would need a separate argument showing that propagation is arrested in time. STR-09’s validated lifespan law concerns prediction over service life, and STR-08’s structural energy storage adds another function to the primary structure; neither roster title establishes the single-member containment property.

Beyond the roster, robustness, alternate load paths, connection ductility and collapse isolation are relevant neighboring ideas. The supplied review mentions a 2024 paper titled “Arresting failure propagation in buildings through collapse isolation,” but supplies neither its contents nor a source URL. Its mechanism, demonstrated scope and implications for STR-12’s novelty therefore remain unresolved.

unresolved_issues: Whether an existing structural system already provides the proposed ordinary-cost capability across a clearly defined building class is not established by the supplied evidence.
Building-code adoption and the research frontier through November 1, 2026 remain unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The detailed provisions of ASCE/SEI 76-23 cannot be independently assessed from the supplied collection because the standard itself was not captured.
The 2025 review’s detailed conclusions about special seismic detailing and particular configurations remain unavailable in the retained subscription preview.
The earlier prestressed-steel corner-removal assertion requires identifiable test evidence; its absence here does not establish that the assertion is false.
The proposed building class, load envelope, wall-segment definition, permitted collapse region, construction-error range and affordability threshold remain to be specified.
STR-07’s full definition and the contents of the referenced 2024 collapse-isolation paper are needed to assess overlap and novelty.

brief.title: Buildings that contain collapse after losing a support
possible: People could occupy affordable buildings designed to keep damage local if any single main support suddenly failed. Losing a column or a defined section of supporting wall would leave any collapse confined to an area specified in advance.
Engineers could apply a general design principle across a defined class of buildings, without separately studying every possible support loss on every project.
why: A local failure can spread until much of a building collapses. Containing that spread would give building occupants protection against a much larger structural failure.
Making this protection part of ordinary construction would help engineers apply it consistently. A general design principle could also reduce the work needed to assess individual buildings.

sources.who: NIST and the American Society of Civil Engineers
sources.showed: NIST tested building structures and used the results to check computer simulations of support loss. This research informed a standard that sets goals for limiting collapse and lets engineers choose how to meet them.
sources.quote: The experiments were useful for identifying the degree that beams and connections can rotate and bend before a structure is overwhelmed and crumbles.
sources.cited_for: Physical tests and computer models underpin existing methods for assessing whether local failures will spread.
sources.not_established: These methods do not establish affordable containment after every qualifying loss of a main support.

sources.who: American Society of Civil Engineers Structural Engineering Institute
sources.showed: This is a building design standard for limiting collapse that spreads far beyond the initial structural damage.
sources.cited_for: It provides a framework for designing against the spread of local structural failures.
sources.not_established: A design framework does not itself demonstrate containment after every qualifying support loss at ordinary construction cost.

sources.who: American Society of Civil Engineers Structural Engineering Institute
sources.showed: The engineering institute released a consensus standard covering design, assessment, construction and testing to limit the spread of collapse.
sources.quote: The American Society of Civil Engineers Structural Engineering Institute has released the nation’s first consensus-based document specifically developed as a design aid for the resistance of disproportionate collapse in buildings and other structures.
sources.cited_for: The standard gives engineers a shared process for designing buildings to resist spreading collapse.
sources.not_established: The standard's release does not demonstrate a general structural system that contains every qualifying support loss.

sources.showed: Their review identifies a gap in earthquake design: failures that spread after local damage are not systematically included in standard procedures.
sources.quote: Consequently, its occurrence during major earthquakes—often considered rare—has not been systematically included in standard seismic design procedures.
sources.cited_for: Earthquake damage needs explicit consideration when assessing whether local failures can spread.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate containment after any support loss in an earthquake-damaged building.

shown: NIST researchers have tested parts of buildings and entire structures, then used those experiments to check computer models of structural failure. Their work helped inform an American Society of Civil Engineers standard for limiting how far collapse spreads.
This establishes methods for assessing specified damage scenarios. An affordable system with demonstrated containment after any qualifying loss of a main support remains the goal.
missing: A validated explanation of why redirected loads stop collapse from spreading across the full claimed range of buildings and support locations.
Repeatable tests covering corner columns, supporting-wall sections and realistic construction errors.
Evidence that ordinary construction methods meet a stated cost target while preserving containment.

milestones.label: Sudden support losses leave collapse inside predefined boundaries
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to keep collapse within preset boundaries after varied sudden support losses in multistory frames and supporting-wall buildings under stated loads. This would demonstrate containment across different support layouts.

milestones.label: Repeatable tests account for damage and construction errors
milestones.explanation: Repeatable tests would have to account for damage from earlier tests and include specified construction errors. This would establish whether containment depends on unusually precise construction or a specimen's damage history.

milestones.label: A validated explanation covers every qualifying support loss
milestones.explanation: A structural explanation challenged by experiments and tested computer models would have to cover every qualifying support loss within the stated scope. This would justify extending the claim beyond the cases physically tested.

milestones.label: Ordinary construction meets stated costs and containment limits
milestones.explanation: Construction evidence would have to meet a stated cost baseline using ordinary methods and identify where containment remains unproven. This would establish affordability and define the protection people could rely on.

uncertain: Which building types, loads, wall-section sizes, construction errors and collapse boundaries should the claim cover?
What additional cost would still count as affordable ordinary construction?
Containment alone would not establish safe occupancy; fire, foundation failure and multiple support losses require separate demonstrations.

page.title: Disproportionate collapse resistance after single-support loss
page.definition: A structural design rule would confine collapse after sudden loss of any one primary support throughout a declared class of buildings. Primary supports comprise columns, beams supporting columns, and defined lengths of load-bearing wall.

goal.need: The Oklahoma City bombing initially destroyed three columns of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building; subsequent collapse affected nearly half the building. Limiting failure propagation addresses this amplification of damage. The single-support target concerns a smaller initiating failure than this incident and does not establish resistance to the complete blast.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: keep small, isolated failures in a structure from propagating and bringing down the entire building or a major part of it
statements.context: NIST describes the purpose of ASCE/SEI 76-23.

statements.quote: to develop a novel fuse-based segmentation design approach to limit or arrest the propagation of failures in building structures subjected to extreme events.
statements.context: Objective of grant 101000396, signed on 12 January 2021. Segmentation divides a building into parts so that failure in one part can be isolated.

statements.body: European Commission Joint Research Centre, expert report
statements.quote: Robustness should be (at minimum) an intrinsic property of the structural system.
statements.context: The report’s assessment of gaps in existing robustness provisions.

completion.title: A validated design rule bounds collapse after every single-support loss throughout a declared building class.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed rule, validated by physical tests, establishes stability after sudden removal of each supporting column, each beam supporting columns, or each nominal load-bearing wall length, one at a time at every storey, throughout declared geometry, material, accidental-loading and construction-tolerance ranges. Floor collapse at any storey is limited to the smaller of 15% of that storey’s floor area and 100 m², and extends no further than the immediately adjacent storeys. Wall lengths follow Approved Document A, paragraph 5.3. The rule establishes coverage without separately analysing every removal location in each project.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; the damage limits and support definitions come from England’s Approved Document A, paragraphs 5.1d and 5.3.
completion.basis: Searched Approved Document A, UFC 4-023-03, JRC’s 2024 guidance, public descriptions of ASCE/SEI 76-23 and Endure’s objectives. Found no acceptance test for a class-wide rule replacing project-specific removal checks. The proposed test retains England’s published damage limits and adds class-wide coverage. Existing tie rules and permission to analyse equivalent locations together do not establish that stronger property.

milestones.title: A structural assembly carries its required horizontal tie force through 0.20 rad rotation.
milestones.criterion: Where beams and connections supply horizontal ties, they carry the applicable UFC longitudinal, transverse or peripheral tie demand at 0.20 rad rotation. In NIST’s 2011 tests of two full-scale reinforced-concrete assemblies, bottom reinforcement first fractured at about 0.179 rad and 547 kN in the intermediate moment frame, and about 0.20 rad and 1,232 kN in the special moment frame. These static pushdown results establish deformation capacities, not compliance with every required tie demand.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Defense, UFC 4-023-03, sections 3-1 and 3-1.4; applicable when structural members provide horizontal ties.
milestones.threshold_quote: tie force magnitudes while undergoing rotations of 0.20-rad (11.3-deg)

milestones.title: A building bridges prescribed sudden support losses within UFC force and deformation capacities.
milestones.criterion: The UFC nonlinear dynamic assessment uses G = 1.2D + (0.5L or 0.2S), with D, L and S denoting dead, live and snow loads. Removal takes less than 0.1 times the damaged structure’s relevant vertical period. At prescribed column and wall locations, expected deformation capacities exceed maximum demands; reduced lower-bound strengths meet force demands; stability is retained. UFC Appendix E illustrates the assessment with one four-storey steel-building design and three representative column-removal locations.
milestones.set_by: United States Department of Defense, UFC 4-023-03, sections 3-2.9, 3-2.10 and 3-2.13.
milestones.threshold_quote: expected deformation capacities greater than the maximum calculated deformation demands.

milestones.title: A full-scale building arrests collapse at predefined borders after three column removals.
milestones.criterion: In the published precast-frame protocol, remove two penultimate-edge columns quasi-statically, then dynamically remove the intervening corner column. Impose 11.8 kN/m² on the bays expected to collapse. Collapse remains within the predefined segment, with connection failures preceding further column failures. Reported on 15 May 2024: one 15 m × 12 m, two-storey specimen arrested collapse at its designated border. This demonstrates that specimen and damage sequence.
milestones.set_by: Universitat Politècnica de València Endure team, Makoond et al.’s published full-scale experimental protocol; written for a precast reinforced-concrete frame.
milestones.threshold_quote: the collapse following a large initial failure is always restricted to components immediately adjacent to those directly involved in the initial failure

milestones.title: A building passes every Class 2b support-removal check within the 15% or 100 m² collapse limit.
milestones.criterion: Use Approved Document A’s Class 2b notional-removal alternative: check each column, each beam supporting columns and any nominal wall length, one at a time in each storey. The building remains stable; floor area at risk is at most min(15% of that storey’s area, 100 m²), without extending beyond immediately adjacent storeys. Wall lengths follow paragraph 5.3. Key-element strengthening alone does not demonstrate this removal result. On 15 June 2026, Setiawan et al. reported a three-storey concrete-building model preventing collapse after any single-column loss; this does not establish the wall and transfer-beam checks.
milestones.set_by: England’s Department for Communities and Local Government, Approved Document A, paragraph 5.1d; the notional-removal option for Consequence Class 2b buildings.
milestones.threshold_quote: does not exceed 15% of the floor area of that storey

not_found: No published numerical affordability threshold or construction-tolerance envelope was located for the class-wide claim.
The full text of ASCE/SEI 76-23 and the supplied Engineering News-Record article could not be opened.
The supplied earthquake-review page exposed its abstract but not its subscription full text.

results.finding: One retrofitted steel joint sustained the UFC-required tie force at 0.216 rad under static loading.
results.detail: The reported tie forces exceed the calculated UFC demand at fracture, but the text does not state the force at exactly 0.20 rad.
results.quote:
The specimen sustained a 
maximum vertical force of 148 kN at a beam rotation of 0.216 rad, greater than the target of 
0.2 rad, as indicated in Fig. 18 with a dashed line.

results.finding: One full-scale precast building arrested collapse at its designated border after three column removals.
results.detail: The 15 m × 12 m, two-storey specimen carried 11.8 kN/m² on the bays expected to collapse. Two penultimate-edge columns were removed quasi-statically, then the intervening corner column dynamically. Connection failures preceded any column failures.
results.quote: Following the removal of two penultimate-edge columns in phase 1, the sudden removal of the C12 corner column in phase 2 triggered a collapse that was arrested along the border delineated by columns C3, C7, C6 and C10

results.finding: One three-storey concrete building model withstood loss of any single column.
results.detail: The result covers single-column removal but does not establish the required checks for beams supporting columns or nominal wall lengths.
results.quote:
As such, we verified that the adaptive continuity design could withstand the loss of a single column from any possible location, just as the unsegmented building could (Supplementary Fig.
2
; Supplementary Movie
3
).

results.finding: One retrofitted steel-joint subassembly sustained approximately 100% of the UFC load combination after simulated column loss.
results.detail: The test used a scaled, restrained subassembly, not a building-wide UFC nonlinear dynamic assessment. It does not establish the prescribed removal locations, removal-time requirement, or all force and deformation checks.
results.quote:
In Specimen 6, as shown in Fig. 24d, the proposed connection was able to withstand the 
initial load, i.e. 78.1 kN on each side or approximately 100% of the UFC load combination, 
after the column was set free to fall.

results.finding: One full-scale precast concrete building prevented collapse after removal of two edge columns.
results.detail: The columns were removed quasi-statically. The test does not establish the UFC nonlinear dynamic assessment’s removal timing, loading, force and deformation capacity checks.
results.quote: Collapse initiation was completely prevented after the removal of two penultimate-edge columns in phase 1 of testing

results.finding: One full-scale precast concrete building prevented collapse after removal of two edge columns.
results.detail: The two columns were removed quasi-statically. The result does not establish checks of every column, beam supporting columns and nominal wall length at every storey.
results.quote: Collapse initiation was completely prevented after the removal of two penultimate-edge columns in phase 1 of testing

results.finding: One simulated three-storey building withstood single-column losses, with vertical displacement up to 190 mm.
results.detail: The authors report checking single-column loss at every location, but the supplied text does not establish all prescribed UFC loading, removal-time, force, deformation and stability requirements, including wall removals.
results.quote: As such, we verified that the adaptive continuity design could withstand the loss of a single column from any possible location, just as the unsegmented building could

results.finding: Of two scaled reinforced-concrete subassemblies, one achieved controlled disconnection and prevented further column damage.
results.detail: The successful test used a quasi-static loading protocol and simulated boundary conditions. The more flexibly restrained specimen did not activate its fuses and approached column failure. Neither was a full-scale building tested under the specified three-column removal protocol.

results.finding: Four half-scale beam-column assemblies reached ultimate chord rotations of at least 0.22 rad.
results.detail: The paper reports that all four exceeded the required peripheral tie force, but compares the requirement with peak vertical load. It does not establish the horizontal tie force carried at 0.20 rad.
results.quote: 0.20 radian rotational capacity requirement of DoD (2010) could be satisfied
